title: Vectors, Components & Products
bulletsLatex: A vector has magnitude and direction; resolve it into perpendicular components with $A_x = A\cos\theta$ and $A_y = A\sin\theta$.
The dot product is a scalar (max when parallel, zero when perpendicular); the cross product is a vector (max when perpendicular, zero when parallel).
trapLatex: Exam Trap: $\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B} = -\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{A}$ (anticommutative). Reversing the order flips the direction, so don't drop the sign.

title: Dimensional Analysis & Limiting Cases
bulletsLatex: Every term in an equation must share the same units; if one term has units of energy, every other term must too.
Check a symbolic answer by letting a variable approach $0$ or $\infty$ — the expression should reduce to a known, sensible result.
trapLatex: Exam Trap: A dimensionless constant like $2\pi$ or $\frac{1}{2}$ carries no units, so it can never fix a dimensional mismatch.

promptLatex: Given two vectors $\mathbf{A} = 3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j}$ and $\mathbf{B} = 4\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}$, what is their scalar (dot) product $\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B}$?
explanationLatex: Using Cartesian components, $\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B} = A_x B_x + A_y B_y = (3)(4) + (-4)(3) = 12 - 12 = 0$, confirming the two vectors are perpendicular.

promptLatex: Vector $\mathbf{a}$ points in the $+x$-direction ($\hat{i}$) and vector $\mathbf{b}$ points in the $+y$-direction ($\hat{j}$). In what direction does the cross product $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$ point?
explanationLatex: By the right-hand rule, pointing your index finger along $+x$ and curling toward $+y$ points your thumb in the $+z$-direction ($\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = +\hat{k}$).

promptLatex: If $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$ for two non-parallel vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, which expression equals $\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a}$?
explanationLatex: The vector (cross) product is anticommutative: reversing the order reverses the right-hand rule direction, so $\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a} = -(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) = -\mathbf{c}$.

promptLatex: A variable force exerted during time interval $\Delta t$ changes the speed of mass $m$ from $v_0$ to $v_f$. Using dimensional analysis ($1\text{ W} = 1\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^3$), which expression has units of average power?
explanationLatex: Power is energy per unit time: $[m v^2 / \Delta t] = \text{kg}\cdot(\text{m/s})^2 / \text{s} = \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^3 = \text{W}$. Choice 2 has units of force (N), and Choice 3 has units of action ($\text{J}\cdot\text{s}$).

promptLatex: An object falling through air experiences a linear drag force $F_{\text{drag}} = -bv$. What are the SI base units of the drag coefficient $b$?
explanationLatex: Solve for $[b] = [F]/[v] = (\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2) / (\text{m/s}) = \text{kg/s}$.

promptLatex: In the elastic potential energy formula $U_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$, what are the SI base units of the spring constant $k$?
explanationLatex: $[k] = [U_s]/[x^2] = (\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2)/\text{m}^2 = \text{kg/s}^2$ (equivalent to $\text{N/m}$).

promptLatex: From Newton's law of universal gravitation $F = \frac{Gm_1 m_2}{r^2}$, what are the SI base units of the gravitational constant $G$?
explanationLatex: $[G] = \frac{[F][r^2]}{[m^2]} = \frac{(\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}^2)(\text{m}^2)}{\text{kg}^2} = \frac{\text{m}^3}{\text{kg}\cdot\text{s}^2}$.

promptLatex: Which expression for the period $T$ of a simple pendulum of mass $m$ and length $L$ in gravitational field $g$ is dimensionally consistent with time?
explanationLatex: $[\sqrt{L/g}] = \sqrt{\text{m} / (\text{m/s}^2)} = \sqrt{\text{s}^2} = \text{s}$. Including $m$ leaves an uncancelled $\sqrt{\text{kg}}$.

promptLatex: Two nonzero vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ satisfy $|\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B}| = \mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B}$. What is the angle $\theta$ between $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$?
explanationLatex: $AB\sin\theta = AB\cos\theta \implies \tan\theta = 1$, which gives $\theta = 45^\circ$ ($\pi/4\text{ rad}$).

promptLatex: Two vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ each have magnitude $5.0$ and form an angle of $60^\circ$ when placed tail-to-tail. What is the magnitude $|\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}|$?
explanationLatex: By the law of cosines (or recognizing an equilateral triangle), $|\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}| = \sqrt{5^2 + 5^2 - 2(5)(5)\cos 60^\circ} = \sqrt{50 - 25} = 5.0$.

promptLatex: A velocity vector of magnitude $v$ is directed at an angle $\phi$ measured clockwise from the $+y$-axis in the first quadrant. What are its Cartesian components $(v_x, v_y)$?
explanationLatex: Because $\phi$ is measured from the $+y$-axis rather than $+x$, the $x$-component is opposite $\phi$ ($v\sin\phi$) and the $y$-component is adjacent ($v\cos\phi$).

promptLatex: In an ideal Atwood machine with masses $m_1$ and $m_2$, which expression for the magnitude of acceleration $a$ passes the limiting-case test when $m_1 = m_2$ and when $m_2 \gg m_1$?
explanationLatex: When $m_1 = m_2$, the system is balanced so $a$ must equal $0$ (eliminates Choices 2 and 4). When $m_2 \gg m_1$, $m_2$ approaches free fall so $a \to g$, matching $g|m_2 - m_1|/(m_1 + m_2)$.

promptLatex: What is the cross product $\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B}$ of $\mathbf{A} = 2\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ and $\mathbf{B} = -\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$?
explanationLatex: Notice that $\mathbf{A} = -2\mathbf{B}$, so the vectors are antiparallel ($\theta = 180^\circ$). Since $\sin 180^\circ = 0$, $\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{0}$.

promptLatex: Which vector is a unit vector pointing in the exact same direction as $\mathbf{r} = 3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j}$?
explanationLatex: Divide $\mathbf{r}$ by its magnitude $|\mathbf{r}| = \sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2} = 5$: $\hat{r} = \frac{3}{5}\hat{i} - \frac{4}{5}\hat{j} = 0.6\hat{i} - 0.8\hat{j}$.

promptLatex: For very small angles $\theta \ll 1\text{ rad}$, $\cos\theta \approx 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2}$. Which expression approximates $1 - \cos\theta$ in this limit?
explanationLatex: Substituting $\cos\theta \approx 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2}$ gives $1 - \left(1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2}\right) = \frac{\theta^2}{2}$.

promptLatex: A particle's position is modeled by $x(t) = A t^3 + B e^{-ct}$, where $x$ is in meters and $t$ is in seconds. What are the SI units of $A$ and $c$?
explanationLatex: Each added term must have units of meters ($[A]\text{s}^3 = \text{m} \implies [A] = \text{m/s}^3$), and the exponent $-ct$ must be dimensionless ($[c]\text{s} = 1 \implies [c] = \text{s}^{-1}$).

promptLatex: Order the steps to find the angle $\theta$ between two 3D vectors $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ given in Cartesian components:
stepsLatex: Compute the dot product $\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B} = A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z$
Compute the magnitudes $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2}$ and $B = \sqrt{B_x^2 + B_y^2 + B_z^2}$
Substitute into $\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B}}{AB}$
Take the inverse cosine: $\theta = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B}}{AB}\right)$
explanationLatex: Combining the component and geometric definitions of the dot product isolates $\cos\theta$ cleanly without needing a 3D cross product.

promptLatex: Order Barron's recommended sequence for verifying a symbolic multiple-choice answer before doing lengthy algebra:
stepsLatex: Check the SI units of each answer choice and eliminate any with the wrong dimension
Test extreme values of system parameters (such as $m \to 0$, $\theta \to 0$, or $r \to \infty$)
Check whether any irrelevant parameter appears in an option
Confirm the sign or direction of the surviving expression
explanationLatex: Dimensional analysis and limiting-case checks often eliminate 3 out of 4 or 4 out of 5 AP Physics C multiple-choice options in seconds.

promptLatex: If two vectors $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$ are perpendicular, what is $|\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{Q}|^2 - |\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Q}|^2$?
explanationLatex: Because $\mathbf{P} \perp \mathbf{Q}$, both $\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Q}$ form the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs $P$ and $Q$, so both squared magnitudes equal $P^2 + Q^2$ and their difference is $0$.

promptLatex: What is the scalar component of force $\mathbf{F} = (10\hat{i} - 5\hat{j})\text{ N}$ along the unit direction $\hat{u} = 0.6\hat{i} + 0.8\hat{j}$?
explanationLatex: The scalar projection along a unit vector is $F_u = \mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{u} = (10)(0.6) + (-5)(0.8) = 6.0 - 4.0 = 2.0\text{ N}$.

title: Motion, Graphs & Calculus
bulletsLatex: On a position-time graph, slope is velocity; on a velocity-time graph, slope is acceleration and signed area is displacement.
For non-uniform acceleration you cannot use the constant-$a$ formulas — integrate $a(t)$ once for $v(t)$ and again for $x(t)$.
trapLatex: Exam Trap: Speed is the magnitude of velocity $|v|$; a negative velocity does not mean slowing down. Speeding up requires $v$ and $a$ to share the same sign.

title: Projectile Motion & Circular Motion
bulletsLatex: Horizontal and vertical projectile motions are independent: horizontal velocity is constant, vertical motion is free fall.
In circular motion the centripetal component $v^2/r$ changes direction; a tangential component $a_t$ changes speed.
trapLatex: Exam Trap: At the apex of projectile motion the vertical velocity is zero, but the horizontal velocity (and thus the speed) is generally NOT zero.

promptLatex: The position of an object is given by $x(t) = 2 + 4t - t^2$, where $x$ is in meters and $t$ is in seconds. What is the particle's average acceleration from $t = 0$ to $t = 2\text{ s}$?
explanationLatex: Differentiating twice gives $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt} = 4 - 2t$ and $a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = -2\text{ m/s}^2$. Since acceleration is constant, the average acceleration over any interval is $-2\text{ m/s}^2$.

promptLatex: A $400\text{ kg}$ car accelerates from rest to a final speed $v$ over a distance $d$. Assuming the same constant acceleration, what speed does the car reach from rest over a distance $2d$?
explanationLatex: From $v_f^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$ with $v_0 = 0$, $v_f = \sqrt{2ad} \propto \sqrt{d}$. Doubling the distance increases speed by $\sqrt{2}$.

promptLatex: Two objects start at different positions and move along the $x$-axis. Between $t = 0$ and $t = t_f$, the area under their $v(t)$ graphs is identical. Which quantity must be the same for both objects over $[0, t_f]$?
optionsLatex: Both total displacement and average velocity
explanationLatex: The signed area under $v(t)$ equals total displacement $\Delta x = \int_0^{t_f} v(t)\,dt$. Since $\Delta x$ and $\Delta t = t_f$ are identical, average velocity $\bar{v} = \Delta x / t_f$ must also be identical.

promptLatex: The velocity of a particle moving in 1D is $v(t) = 4 + 3t^2$ (in $\text{m/s}$). What is its average velocity on the interval $t = 0$ to $t = 2\text{ s}$?

An object is dropped from rest ($v(0)=0$) and falls downward under gravity and air resistance, smoothly approaching terminal velocity $v_t$. Which description matches its downward position graph $y(t)$?
optionsLatex: Starts with zero slope, curves concave-up initially, and approaches a straight line of constant positive slope $v_t$
Starts with steep slope and curves concave-down to a horizontal asymptote
Increases linearly with constant slope from $t = 0$
Forms a symmetric parabola opening downward
explanationLatex: The slope of $y(t)$ is $v(t)$. Since $v(0) = 0$ and $v(t)$ increases toward $v_t$, $y(t)$ starts flat, steepens (concave up), and asymptotically becomes a straight line with slope $v_t$.

promptLatex: Three projectiles $A$, $B$, and $C$ are launched over level ground and reach the exact same maximum height $H$, with horizontal ranges $R_A < R_B < R_C$. Which projectile spends the most time in the air?
optionsLatex: All three spend the exact same amount of time in the air
explanationLatex: Time of flight depends solely on vertical motion. Reaching the same maximum height $H$ requires the same initial vertical velocity $v_{0y} = \sqrt{2gH}$, giving the same flight time $t = 2\sqrt{2H/g}$.

promptLatex: Two boats start at the same dock and move with constant velocities $\mathbf{v}_1 = (3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j})\text{ m/s}$ and $\mathbf{v}_2 = (-1\hat{i} + 5\hat{j})\text{ m/s}$. At what rate is the distance between them increasing?
explanationLatex: The relative velocity vector is $\mathbf{v}_{12} = \mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2 = (3 - (-1))\hat{i} + (2 - 5)\hat{j} = 4\hat{i} - 3\hat{j}$. Its magnitude is $\sqrt{4^2 + (-3)^2} = 5\text{ m/s}$.

promptLatex: A particle moves along a curved path with a nonzero tangential acceleration $a_t = +cv$ (parallel to $\mathbf{v}$) and a nonzero normal acceleration $a_n$. Which statement is true?
optionsLatex: The particle's speed is increasing while its direction of motion is changing
The particle must be moving in a circle of constant radius
The net acceleration is perpendicular to velocity
explanationLatex: A tangential component parallel to $\mathbf{v}$ increases speed ($dv/dt > 0$), while a perpendicular component changes the direction of $\mathbf{v}$ along any curved path (not necessarily a circle).

promptLatex: At a certain instant, a particle moving on a circular track in the $xy$-plane has velocity in the $+y$-direction and acceleration with components in both the $+x$ and $+y$ directions. How is the particle moving?
explanationLatex: With $\mathbf{v}$ along $+y$, $+a_y$ is parallel to $\mathbf{v}$ (speeding up), and $+a_x$ points toward the center of curvature to the right, which corresponds to clockwise motion.

promptLatex: If the angular position of a rotating disk is given by $\theta(t) = 2 + 4t - 3t^2$, what is its angular velocity $\omega(t)$?
explanationLatex: Angular velocity is the time derivative of angular position: $\omega(t) = \frac{d\theta}{dt} = 4 - 6t$.

promptLatex: A particle moves along the $x$-axis with acceleration $a(t) = 6t - 2\text{ m/s}^2$. If $v(0) = 3\text{ m/s}$, what is its velocity at $t = 2\text{ s}$?
A particle starts at $x(0) = 0$ with velocity $v(t) = 12t^2 - 6t$ (in $\text{m/s}$). At what time $t > 0$ does the particle return to the origin $x = 0$?
explanationLatex: $x(t) = \int_0^t (12\tau^2 - 6\tau)\,d\tau = 4t^3 - 3t^2 = t^2(4t - 3)$. Setting $x(t) = 0$ for $t > 0$ yields $t = \frac{3}{4} = 0.75\text{ s}$.

promptLatex: A projectile is launched over level ground at speed $v_0$ and angle $\theta$ ($0 < \theta < 90^\circ$). What is the instantaneous radius of curvature $R_c$ of its parabolic path at the very top (apex) of its trajectory?
explanationLatex: At the apex, $v_y = 0$ so speed is $v = v_0\cos\theta$, and acceleration $g$ is completely perpendicular to $\mathbf{v}$. Setting $a_c = g = \frac{v^2}{R_c}$ gives $R_c = \frac{v_0^2\cos^2\theta}{g}$.

promptLatex: A swimmer with speed $v_s$ in still water wants to cross a river of width $W$ flowing at speed $v_r < v_s$ in the **shortest possible time**. How should the swimmer aim, and what is the crossing time?
optionsLatex: Aim straight across perpendicular to the current; $t = \frac{W}{v_s}$
Aim upstream at $\sin\theta = v_r / v_s$; $t = \frac{W}{\sqrt{v_s^2 - v_r^2}}$
Aim straight across perpendicular to the current; $t = \frac{W}{\sqrt{v_s^2 + v_r^2}}$
explanationLatex: Crossing time depends only on the velocity component perpendicular to the banks ($v_\perp$). Maximizing $v_\perp = v_s$ by aiming straight across minimizes time to $t = W/v_s$.

promptLatex: A ball dropped from rest from the roof of a tall building falls a total distance $H$ in time $T$. How far did it fall during the first $T/2$ of its drop?
explanationLatex: For free fall from rest, $y(t) = \frac{1}{2}gt^2 \propto t^2$. At $t = T/2$, $y(T/2) = \frac{1}{2}g(T/2)^2 = \frac{1}{4}H$.

promptLatex: A particle starts from rest at $x = 0$ and moves with position-dependent acceleration $a(x) = kx$, where $k$ is a positive constant. What is its speed $v(x)$?
explanationLatex: Use $a = v\frac{dv}{dx} = kx \implies \int_0^v v'\,dv' = \int_0^x kx'\,dx' \implies \frac{1}{2}v^2 = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 \implies v(x) = \sqrt{k}\,x$.

promptLatex: A bead slides along a circular wire of radius $R$ with constant angular acceleration $\alpha$. At the instant its speed is $v$, what is the magnitude of its total acceleration?
explanationLatex: Tangential acceleration is $a_t = \alpha R$ and centripetal acceleration is $a_r = v^2/R$. Since they are perpendicular, $a_{\text{total}} = \sqrt{a_t^2 + a_r^2}$.

promptLatex: Order the steps to derive $x(t)$ for a particle with acceleration $a(t) = bt$ given $v(0) = v_0$ and $x(0) = x_0$:
stepsLatex: Integrate acceleration over time: $v(t) = v_0 + \int_0^t b\tau\,d\tau$
Evaluate the velocity function: $v(t) = v_0 + \frac{1}{2}bt^2$
Integrate velocity over time: $x(t) = x_0 + \int_0^t \left(v_0 + \frac{1}{2}b\tau^2\right)d\tau$
Obtain the final position function: $x(t) = x_0 + v_0 t + \frac{1}{6}bt^3$
explanationLatex: When acceleration is non-uniform, constant-acceleration kinematics formulas fail—you must integrate $a(t)$ to get $v(t)$, then integrate $v(t)$ to get $x(t)$.

promptLatex: Order the steps to derive the horizontal range $R$ of a projectile launched at speed $v_0$ and angle $\theta$ over level ground:
stepsLatex: Decompose initial velocity into $v_{0x} = v_0\cos\theta$ and $v_{0y} = v_0\sin\theta$
Set vertical displacement $y(t) = (v_0\sin\theta)t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = 0$ to solve for flight time $t = \frac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}$
Substitute $t$ into horizontal displacement: $R = (v_0\cos\theta)\left(\frac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}\right)$
Apply $2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin(2\theta)$ to get $R = \frac{v_0^2\sin(2\theta)}{g}$
explanationLatex: Using the vertical equation to find time of flight and plugging into $x(t) = v_{0x}t$ is the universal template for 2D projectile problems.

promptLatex: Two projectiles are launched simultaneously from the origin with identical horizontal velocity components $v_{1x} = v_{2x}$, but $v_{1y} > v_{2y}$. Both strike a vertical wall at $x = D$ before hitting the ground. Which hits the wall first, and which hits higher?
optionsLatex: They hit at the same time; Projectile 1 hits higher
Projectile 2 hits first; Projectile 1 hits higher
They hit at the same time and at the same height
explanationLatex: Because $v_{1x} = v_{2x}$, both take the exact same time $t = D/v_x$ to reach $x = D$. Since $v_{1y} > v_{2y}$, $y_1(t) = v_{1y}t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 > y_2(t)$.

title: Newton's Laws & Free-Body Diagrams
bulletsLatex: Draw a free-body diagram first: include gravity, normal, tension, applied forces, and friction — never 'invent' a force to balance the picture.
Static friction adjusts up to $\mu_s F_N$ to prevent sliding; kinetic friction is fixed at $\mu_k F_N$ once sliding begins.
trapLatex: Exam Trap: The normal force $F_N$ is not always $mg$. On an incline or with a vertical applied-force component, $F_N$ changes, which in turn changes the friction force.

title: Circular Motion & Resistive Forces
bulletsLatex: Net radial force points toward the center and equals $mv^2/r$; tangential force changes speed. Gravity has both components on a vertical circle.
With linear drag, the equation of motion is a separable differential equation; terminal speed occurs when acceleration (and net force) is zero.
trapLatex: Exam Trap: At terminal velocity the object is NOT motionless — it still moves at constant $v_t$, it just has zero acceleration.

promptLatex: In a two-pulley system, block $m_1$ hangs from a movable pulley supported by two vertical segments of a single rope, while the other end of the rope is tied to hanging block $m_2$. What is the constraint between their accelerations $a_1$ and $a_2$?
explanationLatex: When $m_1$ moves by $\Delta y_1$, both vertical rope segments supporting its pulley shorten by $\Delta y_1$, releasing $2\Delta y_1$ of rope to $m_2$. Differentiating twice gives $a_2 = 2a_1$.

promptLatex: A chain of $N$ identical blocks, each of mass $m$, is pulled to the right across a horizontal surface (coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k$) with acceleration $a$. What is the tension $T_i$ in the string connecting block $i$ (counting from the left) to block $i + 1$?
explanationLatex: Treat blocks $1$ through $i$ as a single system of total mass $im$. Newton's second law gives $T_i - f_k = (im)a \implies T_i - \mu_k(im)g = ima \implies T_i = i(ma + \mu_k mg)$.

promptLatex: A ball attached to a string of length $r$ swings in a vertical circle. At the exact instant the string is horizontal and the ball is moving straight upward with speed $v$, what is the rate of change of the ball's speed ($dv/dt$)?
explanationLatex: Rate of change of speed equals tangential acceleration $a_t$. When the string is horizontal, tension is purely radial ($a_r = v^2/r$), while gravity acts purely tangentially downward opposite to the upward velocity, so $dv/dt = -g$.

promptLatex: A force $F$ directed at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal pulls a block of mass $m$ to the right across a rough floor with coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k$. What is the magnitude of the normal force $F_N$?
explanationLatex: Since there is no vertical acceleration, $\sum F_y = F_N + F\sin\theta - mg = 0 \implies F_N = mg - F\sin\theta$.

promptLatex: A particle of mass $m$ moves along the $x$-axis according to $x(t) = at^4 - bt^3$. What is the net force $F(t)$ acting on the particle?
explanationLatex: Differentiate twice: $v(t) = 4at^3 - 3bt^2$ and $a(t) = 12at^2 - 6bt$. By Newton's second law, $F(t) = ma(t) = m(12at^2 - 6bt)$.

promptLatex: A traffic light hangs in static equilibrium from two cables angled at $\theta_1$ (left) and $\theta_2$ (right) relative to the vertical, with tensions $T_1$ and $T_2$. Which equation expresses horizontal equilibrium?
explanationLatex: Because the angles are measured from the vertical, the horizontal components are $T_1\sin\theta_1$ (left) and $T_2\sin\theta_2$ (right). Setting $\sum F_x = 0$ gives $T_1\sin\theta_1 = T_2\sin\theta_2$.

promptLatex: A car of mass $m$ travels around a circular track of radius $r$ banked at an angle $\theta$. At what speed $v$ is there zero static friction required between the tires and the road?
explanationLatex: Using horizontal and vertical axes: $F_N\cos\theta = mg$ and $F_N\sin\theta = \frac{mv^2}{r}$. Dividing the second equation by the first yields $\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg} \implies v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$.

promptLatex: A car rounds a curve of radius $r$ banked at angle $\theta$ with static friction coefficient $\mu_s$. What is the maximum speed $v_{\max}$ before the car slides up the incline?
explanationLatex: At $v_{\max}$, static friction $f_s = \mu_s F_N$ points down the incline to help keep the car from sliding outward. Setting $\mu_s = 0$ cleanly reduces the expression to $\sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$.

promptLatex: Block $m_1$ rests on a frictionless horizontal airtrack and is connected by a light string over an ideal pulley to a hanging mass $m_2$. What is the tension $T$ in the string while the system accelerates?
explanationLatex: System acceleration is $a = \frac{m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$. Applying $T = m_1 a$ to the block on the airtrack gives $T = \frac{m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2} < m_2 g$.

promptLatex: Riders stand against the inner vertical wall of a spinning cylindrical rotor ride of radius $R$ with coefficient of static friction $\mu_s$. What is the minimum linear speed $v$ required so riders do not slip down when the floor drops?
explanationLatex: The wall's normal force provides centripetal force: $F_N = \frac{mv^2}{R}$. Vertical equilibrium requires $mg = f_s \le \mu_s F_N = \mu_s\frac{mv^2}{R} \implies v_{\min} = \sqrt{\frac{gR}{\mu_s}}$.

promptLatex: A baseball of mass $m_b$ is falling toward Earth of mass $m_E$. If $a_b$ is the acceleration of the baseball due to Earth and $a_E$ is the acceleration of Earth due to the baseball, which statement is true?
optionsLatex: $a_b \gg a_E$, and the accelerations are antiparallel
$a_b \gg a_E$, and the accelerations are parallel
$a_b = a_E$, and the accelerations are antiparallel
explanationLatex: By Newton's third law, Earth and the baseball exert equal and opposite gravitational forces on each other. Since $m_E \gg m_b$, $a_b = F/m_b \gg a_E = F/m_E$, and they point in opposite (antiparallel) directions.

promptLatex: A student of mass $m$ stands on a bathroom scale inside an elevator that is accelerating downward with magnitude $a$ ($a < g$). What normal force does the scale read?
explanationLatex: Taking downward as positive, $\sum F_y = mg - F_N = ma \implies F_N = m(g - a)$. Notice that in free fall ($a = g$), the scale reads $0$.

promptLatex: Two unequal masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ hang on opposite sides of an ideal, frictionless, massless pulley suspended from the ceiling by a pin. What is the upward force $F_{\text{pin}}$ exerted by the pin on the pulley while the masses accelerate?
explanationLatex: The pulley is not translating, so $F_{\text{pin}} = 2T$. Since Atwood tension is $T = \frac{2m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$, $F_{\text{pin}} = \frac{4m_1 m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2}$ (check: when $m_1 = m_2 = m$, $F_{\text{pin}} = 2mg$).

promptLatex: An object of mass $m$ falls through a fluid that exerts a linear resistive drag force $F_{\text{drag}} = -bv$. What is the object's terminal speed $v_t$?
explanationLatex: At terminal speed, acceleration is zero so drag balances gravity: $bv_t = mg \implies v_t = \frac{mg}{b}$.

promptLatex: An object of mass $m$ is released from rest in a medium with drag $F_{\text{drag}} = -bv$, giving $v(t) = v_t(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$. What is the time constant $\tau$?
explanationLatex: From $m\frac{dv}{dt} = mg - bv$, dividing by $m$ gives $\frac{dv}{dt} = g - \frac{b}{m}v$. The exponential rate is $\frac{b}{m}$, so the time constant is $\tau = \frac{m}{b}$ (units: $\text{kg}/(\text{kg/s}) = \text{s}$).

promptLatex: A block of mass $m$ is pushed up a rough incline of angle $\theta$ by a purely horizontal force $F$. What is the normal force $F_N$ exerted by the incline on the block?
explanationLatex: Resolving forces perpendicular to the incline: both $mg\cos\theta$ and $F\sin\theta$ push the block into the surface, so $F_N = mg\cos\theta + F\sin\theta$.

promptLatex: Three blocks of masses $m_1$, $m_2$, and $m_3$ sit in a row on a frictionless table. A horizontal force $F$ pushes $m_1$ to the right. What is the magnitude of the contact force exerted by $m_2$ on $m_3$?
explanationLatex: All three blocks share acceleration $a = \frac{F}{m_1 + m_2 + m_3}$. The only horizontal force on $m_3$ is the contact force from $m_2$, so $F_{2\text{ on }3} = m_3 a = \frac{m_3 F}{m_1 + m_2 + m_3}$.

promptLatex: Order the steps to derive $v(t)$ for an object of mass $m$ falling from rest ($v(0) = 0$) with linear air drag $F_{\text{drag}} = -bv$:
stepsLatex: Write Newton's second law downward: $m\frac{dv}{dt} = mg - bv$
Separate variables: $\frac{dv}{g - (b/m)v} = dt$
Integrate both sides from $0$ to $v$ and $0$ to $t$: $-\frac{m}{b}\ln\!\left(\frac{g - (b/m)v}{g}\right) = t$
Exponentiate and solve for $v(t)$: $v(t) = \frac{mg}{b}\left(1 - e^{-(b/m)t}\right)$
explanationLatex: Separating variables in $m\frac{dv}{dt} = mg - bv$ is one of the highest-yield calculus derivations on the AP Physics C Mechanics FRQ section.

promptLatex: Order the steps to derive the frictionless banked-curve speed $v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$:
stepsLatex: Choose horizontal ($x$, toward center) and vertical ($y$) axes rather than tilted axes
Write vertical equilibrium: $F_N\cos\theta - mg = 0 \implies F_N = \frac{mg}{\cos\theta}$
Write radial centripetal force equation: $F_N\sin\theta = \frac{mv^2}{r}$
Substitute $F_N$ to get $mg\tan\theta = \frac{mv^2}{r} \implies v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$
explanationLatex: Because the car's centripetal acceleration points horizontally toward the center of the circle, keeping axes horizontal and vertical avoids splitting $a_c$ into components.

promptLatex: A skydiver of mass $m$ experiences quadratic air drag $F_{\text{drag}} = cv^2$. If the skydiver carries extra gear that doubles the total mass to $2m$ without changing cross-sectional area (so $c$ stays constant), by what factor does terminal speed $v_t$ change?
explanationLatex: At terminal velocity, $cv_t^2 = mg \implies v_t = \sqrt{\frac{mg}{c}} \propto \sqrt{m}$. Doubling mass increases $v_t$ by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$.

title: Variable Work, Power & Potential Energy
bulletsLatex: Work is the area under a force-position ($F$ vs. $x$) graph; positive work adds kinetic energy, negative work removes it.
Instantaneous power is $P = \frac{dW}{dt} = \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{v} = Fv\cos\theta$; average power is $P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{W}{\Delta t}$.
trapLatex: Exam Trap: A force perpendicular to velocity (like tension in a pendulum or magnetic force) does ZERO work and delivers ZERO instantaneous power.

title: Energy Conservation & Potential Wells
bulletsLatex: Equilibrium occurs where $F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx} = 0$ (local extrema on a $U(x)$ curve): local minima are stable, local maxima are unstable.
For a vertical mass-spring system, measuring $x$ from the hanging equilibrium position lets you ignore $mgy$ and use $U_{\text{tot}} = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$.
trapLatex: Exam Trap: Turning points occur where total mechanical energy $E = U(x)$ ($K = 0$), NOT where $F(x) = 0$.

promptLatex: A person pulls a block of mass $m$ (initially at rest) all the way up an incline of length $d$ and angle $\theta$, then lets it slide halfway back down ($d/2$) before pulling to stop it there. If kinetic friction is $\mu_k$, what is the total work done by the person?
explanationLatex: Since $\Delta K = 0$, $W_{\text{person}} + W_g + W_f = 0$. Net height gain is $(d/2)\sin\theta$, so $W_g = -\frac{1}{2}mgd\sin\theta$. Friction opposes motion over total path $d + d/2 = \frac{3}{2}d$, so $W_f = -\frac{3}{2}\mu_k mgd\cos\theta$. Solving gives $W_{\text{person}} = \frac{1}{2}mgd(\sin\theta + 3\mu_k\cos\theta)$.

promptLatex: A projectile of mass $m$ is thrown straight upward, reaches a maximum height $h$, and lands back at its launch height after a total flight time $T$. What is the average power of the gravitational force over the entire trajectory?
explanationLatex: Because gravity is conservative and the projectile returns to its starting height ($\Delta y = 0$), total work done by gravity is $W_g = 0$, making $P_{\text{avg}} = W_g / T = 0$.

promptLatex: Given ONLY the constant net force vector $\mathbf{F}_{\text{net}}$ acting on an object and its net displacement vector $\Delta\mathbf{r}$, which quantity can be determined directly?
optionsLatex: The net change in the object's kinetic energy ($\Delta K$)
The net change in the object's velocity ($\Delta\mathbf{v}$)
The net change in the object's potential energy ($\Delta U$)
explanationLatex: Without knowing the mass $m$, you cannot find $\mathbf{a}$ or $\Delta\mathbf{v}$, and without knowing which forces are conservative, you cannot find $\Delta U$. However, $W_{\text{net}} = \mathbf{F}_{\text{net}}\cdot\Delta\mathbf{r} = \Delta K$ requires no mass.

promptLatex: A particle is launched over level ground with initial speed $v$ at an angle of elevation $\theta$. Using conservation of mechanical energy, what is the maximum height $y_{\max}$ it reaches?
explanationLatex: At the peak, $v_y = 0$ so kinetic energy is $\frac{1}{2}m(v\cos\theta)^2$. Setting $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgy_{\max} + \frac{1}{2}mv^2\cos^2\theta$ gives $y_{\max} = \frac{v^2(1 - \cos^2\theta)}{2g} = \frac{v^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$.

promptLatex: A particle of mass $m$ moves in a 1D conservative system with potential energy $U(x)$. If it is released from rest at $x_0$ where $U(x_0) = U_0$, and the global minimum of the potential well is $U_{\min}$, what is the particle's maximum speed?
explanationLatex: Total energy is $E = U_0$. Kinetic energy is maximized where potential energy is minimized: $\frac{1}{2}mv_{\max}^2 = E - U_{\min} = U_0 - U_{\min}$.

promptLatex: A single 1D force $F(x) = 2 - 4x$ (in newtons, with $x$ in meters) acts on an object as it moves from $x = 2\text{ m}$ to $x = 1\text{ m}$. What is the change in the object's kinetic energy $\Delta K$?
explanationLatex: $\Delta K = W = \int_2^1 (2 - 4x)\,dx = \left[2x - 2x^2\right]_2^1 = (2 - 2) - (4 - 8) = +4\text{ J}$. On $[1, 2]$, $F(x) < 0$ while $\Delta x < 0$, so work is positive.

promptLatex: A falling apple of mass $m$ and Earth of mass $M_E \gg m$ pull on each other gravitationally. At any instant during the fall, how does the rate at which gravity increases the apple's kinetic energy ($P_m$) compare to that of Earth ($P_E$)?
optionsLatex: $P_m \gg P_E$ because the apple has a much larger velocity parallel to the force
$P_m = P_E$ because the gravitational forces are equal and opposite
$P_E \gg P_m$ because Earth has a much larger mass
$P_m = P_E = 0$ because gravity is internal to the apple-Earth system
explanationLatex: Both experience equal force magnitude $F$, so $P = Fv$. Because $m \ll M_E$, the apple accelerates much faster and reaches a vastly larger speed $v_m \gg v_E$, giving $P_m \gg P_E$.

promptLatex: A puck of mass $m$ sliding at speed $v$ in the $+x$-direction is struck by a stick and rebounds in the $-x$-direction with the exact same speed $v$. What is the net work done on the puck during the impact?
explanationLatex: Kinetic energy is a scalar that depends only on speed: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 0$.

promptLatex: Two ideal massless springs with spring constants $k_1$ and $k_2$ are connected end-to-end in series and attached to a block. If the block is pulled a total distance $x$ from equilibrium, what is the magnitude of the restoring force on the block?
explanationLatex: Series springs share the same tension $F = k_1 x_1 = k_2 x_2$ while total stretch is $x = x_1 + x_2 = F\left(\frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2}\right)$, yielding $F = \frac{k_1 k_2}{k_1 + k_2}x$.

promptLatex: A simple pendulum bob of mass $m$ on a string of length $L$ is released from rest at an angle of $60^\circ$ from the vertical. What is the tension $T$ in the string as the bob swings through its lowest point?
explanationLatex: Vertical drop is $\Delta h = L(1 - \cos 60^\circ) = L/2$. Energy gives $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mg(L/2) \implies \frac{mv^2}{L} = mg$. At the bottom, $T - mg = \frac{mv^2}{L} = mg \implies T = 2mg$.

promptLatex: A particle moves in a 1D potential energy field given by $U(x) = ax^4 - bx^2$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants. At what positive coordinate $x > 0$ is the particle in stable equilibrium?
explanationLatex: Set $F(x) = -\frac{dU}{dx} = -(4ax^3 - 2bx) = 0$. For $x > 0$, $4ax^2 = 2b \implies x = \sqrt{\frac{b}{2a}}$. Since $U''(x) = 12ax^2 - 2b = 4b > 0$, it is a local minimum (stable).

promptLatex: A block of mass $m$ starts from rest at vertical height $h$ on a rough incline of angle $\theta$ and coefficient of kinetic friction $\mu_k$. What is its speed $v$ at the bottom of the incline?
explanationLatex: Ramp length is $L = h/\sin\theta$. Energy balance: $mgh - \mu_k mg\cos\theta\left(\frac{h}{\sin\theta}\right) = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \implies v = \sqrt{2gh(1 - \mu_k\cot\theta)}$.

promptLatex: A mass $m$ is attached to a vertical spring of constant $k$ and lowered slowly until it hangs at rest a distance $d = mg/k$ below the unstretched position. If it is then pulled down an additional distance $A$ and released, what is its maximum kinetic energy?
explanationLatex: Setting $U = 0$ at the hanging equilibrium position cancels the linear $mgx$ gravity term against $-kd\,x$, leaving pure harmonic potential energy $U_{\text{eff}}(y) = \frac{1}{2}ky^2$, so $K_{\max} = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$.

promptLatex: A truck of mass $m$ drives up a long hill inclined at angle $\theta$ at constant speed $v$ against a constant aerodynamic drag force $f_d$. What mechanical power must the engine deliver to the wheels?
explanationLatex: At constant speed, net force along the incline is zero, so $F_{\text{drive}} = mg\sin\theta + f_d$. Instantaneous power is $P = F_{\text{drive}}v = (mg\sin\theta + f_d)v$.

promptLatex: A conservative restoring force in 1D is given by $F(x) = -\alpha x^3$, where $\alpha > 0$. Defining $U(0) = 0$, what is the potential energy function $U(x)$?
explanationLatex: $U(x) - U(0) = -\int_0^x F(x')\,dx' = -\int_0^x (-\alpha x'^3)\,dx' = +\frac{1}{4}\alpha x^4$.

promptLatex: A particle with total mechanical energy $E$ moves in a 1D potential well $U(x)$ with no friction. Which condition defines a classical turning point $x_t$?
explanationLatex: At a turning point, kinetic energy momentarily drops to zero ($K = E - U(x_t) = 0$), while a nonzero slope $dU/dx \ne 0$ provides the restoring force that reverses the particle's velocity.

promptLatex: Order the steps to derive the 1D Work-Energy Theorem $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$ from Newton's second law:
stepsLatex: Start with net work definition: $W_{\text{net}} = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F_{\text{net}}\,dx = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} m\frac{dv}{dt}\,dx$
Apply the chain rule $\frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{dv}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt} = v\frac{dv}{dx}$
Cancel $dx$ to change the variable of integration to velocity: $W_{\text{net}} = \int_{v_1}^{v_2} mv\,dv$
Evaluate the definite integral: $W_{\text{net}} = \frac{1}{2}mv_2^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_1^2 = \Delta K$
explanationLatex: Using the chain rule $a = v\frac{dv}{dx}$ converts a spatial integral over $dx$ directly into a velocity integral over $dv$.

promptLatex: Order the steps to find the minimum launch speed $v_0$ at the bottom of a frictionless vertical loop of radius $R$ so a block stays on the track at the top:
stepsLatex: Apply Newton's 2nd law at the top of the loop: $mg + F_N = \frac{mv_{\text{top}}^2}{R}$
Set normal force $F_N \to 0$ at the threshold of losing contact: $v_{\text{top}}^2 = gR$
Apply conservation of energy from bottom to top: $\frac{1}{2}mv_0^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv_{\text{top}}^2 + mg(2R)$
Substitute $v_{\text{top}}^2 = gR$ to obtain $v_0 = \sqrt{5gR}$
explanationLatex: Remember that the top of a circle of radius $R$ is at height $h = 2R$ above the bottom, not $R$.

title: Impulse, Momentum & Collisions
bulletsLatex: Total linear momentum $\mathbf{p} = \sum m_i\mathbf{v}_i$ is a vector—always conserve $p_x$ and $p_y$ independently in 2D collisions.
Total kinetic energy is conserved ONLY in elastic collisions; in completely inelastic collisions, objects stick together and lose the maximum possible KE.
trapLatex: Exam Trap: In a ballistic pendulum, NEVER set initial bullet KE equal to final gravitational PE—mechanical energy is lost during the inelastic impact.

title: Center of Mass & Continuous Distributions
bulletsLatex: For a 1D rod with variable density $\lambda(x)$, set $dm = \lambda(x)\,dx$ and integrate both numerator $\int x\,dm$ and denominator $M = \int dm$.
Internal forces (explosions, people pulling a rope on ice) NEVER accelerate the center of mass.
trapLatex: Exam Trap: If a projectile explodes midair into fragments, its center of mass continues along the exact original parabolic trajectory until a fragment hits the ground.

promptLatex: Mass $m_1$ moving in the $+x$-direction at speed $v_1$ collides at the origin with mass $m_2$ moving in the $+y$-direction at speed $v_2$, and the two stick together. What angle $\theta$ does their final velocity make with the $+x$-axis?
explanationLatex: By conservation of momentum, $p_{fx} = m_1 v_1$ and $p_{fy} = m_2 v_2$. Therefore $\tan\theta = \frac{p_{fy}}{p_{fx}} = \frac{m_2 v_2}{m_1 v_1}$.

promptLatex: Stating that the net external force on an object is zero is **exact and universally equivalent** to which statement?
optionsLatex: The object's linear momentum vector $\mathbf{p}$ is constant
The object is in static equilibrium
There are no forces acting on the object
explanationLatex: Newton's second law in general form is $\mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = \frac{d\mathbf{p}}{dt}$. Thus $\mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = \mathbf{0} \iff \mathbf{p} = \text{constant}$ (even for variable-mass systems like rockets).

promptLatex: Mass $m_1$ moving in the $+x$-direction has a glancing collision with a stationary mass $m_2$. After the collision, $m_1$ moves with speed $v_1$ at angle $\theta_1$ above the $+x$-axis, and $m_2$ moves with speed $v_2$ at angle $\theta_2$ below the $+x$-axis ($0 < \theta_1, \theta_2 < 90^\circ$). Which statement is necessarily true?
explanationLatex: Initial $y$-momentum is zero, so $m_1 v_1 \sin\theta_1 = m_2 v_2 \sin\theta_2$. If $m_1 v_1 < m_2 v_2$, we must have $\sin\theta_1 > \sin\theta_2$, meaning $\theta_2 < \theta_1$.

promptLatex: A shell falling vertically explodes in midair into two fragments of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ that strike the level ground at the same instant. If $m_1$ lands a horizontal distance $d_1$ from where the intact shell would have hit, what is the distance between $m_1$ and $m_2$ on the ground?
explanationLatex: The horizontal coordinate of the CM stays at the original impact point: $m_1 d_1 = m_2 d_2 \implies d_2 = d_1\frac{m_1}{m_2}$. Since they land on opposite sides, total separation is $d_1 + d_2 = d_1\left(1 + \frac{m_1}{m_2}\right)$.

promptLatex: A person of mass $m_p$ stands at rest in a canoe of mass $m_c$ motionless in still water. If the person walks forward with speed $v_p$ relative to the water, what is the total kinetic energy of the person-canoe system?
explanationLatex: Momentum conservation gives $m_p v_p = m_c v_c \implies v_c = \frac{m_p}{m_c}v_p$. Summing both kinetic energies: $K = \frac{1}{2}m_p v_p^2 + \frac{1}{2}m_c\left(\frac{m_p v_p}{m_c}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}m_p v_p^2\left(1 + \frac{m_p}{m_c}\right)$.

promptLatex: If an object of constant mass $m$ moves with constant acceleration of magnitude $a$, which statement is ALWAYS true?
optionsLatex: In each second, the magnitude of its linear momentum changes by $ma$
In each second, its speed changes by $a$
Its kinetic energy increases at rate $mav$
The object moves along a parabolic path
explanationLatex: Since $\mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} = m\mathbf{a}$ is constant, $\Delta\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{F}_{\text{net}}\Delta t = m\mathbf{a}\Delta t$. For $\Delta t = 1\text{ s}$, $|\Delta\mathbf{p}| = ma$ (whereas speed doesn't change at the peak of projectile motion).

promptLatex: A $50\text{ kg}$ woman and a $75\text{ kg}$ man stand $10.0\text{ m}$ apart on frictionless ice holding opposite ends of a light rope. If the man pulls on the rope until they collide, how far does the woman slide across the ice?
explanationLatex: Setting the woman's initial position at $x = 0$, $x_{\text{cm}} = \frac{(50)(0) + (75)(10.0)}{50 + 75} = 6.0\text{ m}$. Because there is no external horizontal force, the CM stays fixed and they meet at $x = 6.0\text{ m}$.

promptLatex: A projectile fired off a cliff explodes at $t = 4\text{ s}$ via purely vertical internal forces into a $2\text{ kg}$ fragment and a $1\text{ kg}$ fragment. Before either fragment hits the ground, how does the vertical position $y_{\text{cm}}$ of the two-fragment center of mass compare to the unexploded projectile's path?
optionsLatex: It follows the exact same trajectory as if no explosion had occurred
It is lower because kinetic energy was converted into heat
It is higher because the lighter piece shoots upward faster
It moves horizontally with zero vertical acceleration
explanationLatex: Internal forces cancel in action-reaction pairs, leaving gravity $M\mathbf{g}$ as the sole external force. Thus $\mathbf{a}_{\text{cm}} = \mathbf{g}$ remains completely unchanged.

promptLatex: A bullet of mass $m$ embeds itself into a stationary wooden block of mass $M$ hanging from a string of length $L$, causing the block to swing upward to a maximum height $h$. Which expression gives the bullet's initial speed $v_0$?
explanationLatex: Step 1 (inelastic collision): $mv_0 = (m + M)v_f$. Step 2 (swing up): $\frac{1}{2}(m + M)v_f^2 = (m + M)gh \implies v_f = \sqrt{2gh}$. Combining gives $v_0 = \frac{m+M}{m}\sqrt{2gh}$.

promptLatex: A time-varying force $F(t) = F_0 \sin\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{T}\right)$ acts on a particle from $t = 0$ to $t = T$. What is the total impulse $J$ delivered to the particle?
explanationLatex: $J = \int_0^T F_0\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{T}\right)dt = F_0\left[-\frac{T}{\pi}\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{T}\right)\right]_0^T = -\frac{F_0 T}{\pi}(-1 - 1) = \frac{2F_0 T}{\pi}$.

promptLatex: A thin rod of length $L$ lies along the $x$-axis from $x = 0$ to $x = L$ and has linear mass density $\lambda(x) = \lambda_0 x$. What is the $x$-coordinate of its center of mass?
explanationLatex: $x_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\int_0^L x(\lambda_0 x)\,dx}{\int_0^L \lambda_0 x\,dx} = \frac{\frac{1}{3}\lambda_0 L^3}{\frac{1}{2}\lambda_0 L^2} = \frac{2}{3}L$.

promptLatex: Cart A of mass $m$ moving at speed $v_0$ collides head-on and elastically with an identical stationary Cart B of mass $m$ on a frictionless track. What are their speeds immediately after the collision?
optionsLatex: Cart A stops ($0$), Cart B moves at $v_0$
Cart A rebounds at $v_0 / 2$, Cart B moves at $v_0 / 2$
Cart A stops ($0$), Cart B moves at $\sqrt{2}v_0$
explanationLatex: In a 1D head-on elastic collision between equal masses, the two objects simply exchange velocities: Cart A comes to rest and Cart B leaves with velocity $v_0$.

promptLatex: A bowling ball of mass $M$ rolling at speed $v_0$ has a head-on elastic collision with a stationary ping-pong ball of mass $m \ll M$. Approximately how fast does the ping-pong ball fly off?
explanationLatex: The exact elastic formula gives $v_{2f} = \frac{2M}{M + m}v_0$. In the limit $m \ll M$, $\frac{2M}{M + m} \to 2$, so the light target rebounds at nearly $2v_0$.

promptLatex: A billiard ball of mass $m$ strikes an identical stationary billiard ball in a 2D elastic collision, and both balls move off at nonzero angles $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ relative to the incoming direction. What is the angle $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ between their final velocity vectors?
explanationLatex: For equal masses, momentum conservation gives $\mathbf{v}_0 = \mathbf{v}_{1f} + \mathbf{v}_{2f}$, while KE conservation gives $v_0^2 = v_{1f}^2 + v_{2f}^2$. By the Pythagorean theorem, $\mathbf{v}_{1f} \perp \mathbf{v}_{2f}$ ($90^\circ$).

promptLatex: A bullet of mass $m$ strikes and embeds inside a stationary block of mass $M$ on a frictionless surface. What fraction of the bullet's initial kinetic energy remains in the combined block-bullet system?
explanationLatex: $\frac{K_f}{K_i} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}(m + M)v_f^2}{\frac{1}{2}mv_0^2} = \frac{(m + M)\left(\frac{m}{m+M}v_0\right)^2}{mv_0^2} = \frac{m}{m + M}$.

promptLatex: A $0.20\text{ kg}$ rubber ball strikes a vertical wall perpendicularly at $10\text{ m/s}$ and rebounds straight back at $8.0\text{ m/s}$. What is the magnitude of the impulse exerted by the wall on the ball?
explanationLatex: Momentum is a vector! Taking rebound as positive: $J = m(v_f - v_i) = 0.20\text{ kg}[+8.0 - (-10.0)]\text{ m/s} = 3.6\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$.

promptLatex: Order the steps to derive the center of mass $x_{\text{cm}}$ of a rod of length $L$ with quadratic density $\lambda(x) = \beta x^2$:
stepsLatex: Define a differential mass slice of length $dx$: $dm = \lambda(x)\,dx = \beta x^2\,dx$
Integrate to find total mass: $M = \int_0^L \beta x^2\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\beta L^3$
Integrate the first mass moment: $\int_0^L x\,dm = \int_0^L \beta x^3\,dx = \frac{1}{4}\beta L^4$
Divide to get the center of mass: $x_{\text{cm}} = \frac{\frac{1}{4}\beta L^4}{\frac{1}{3}\beta L^3} = \frac{3}{4}L$
explanationLatex: Always compute $M = \int dm$ separately so the unknown density constant $\beta$ cancels cleanly at the end.

promptLatex: Order the steps to find the muzzle speed $v_0$ of a bullet of mass $m$ fired into a ballistic pendulum of mass $M$ and string length $L$ that swings up to angle $\theta$:
stepsLatex: Conserve linear momentum during the instantaneous collision: $mv_0 = (m + M)v_f$
Express vertical height gain from geometry: $h = L(1 - \cos\theta)$
Conserve mechanical energy during the upward swing: $\frac{1}{2}(m + M)v_f^2 = (m + M)gL(1 - \cos\theta)$
Eliminate $v_f$ to get $v_0 = \left(\frac{m + M}{m}\right)\sqrt{2gL(1 - \cos\theta)}$
explanationLatex: Splitting a collision-plus-swing problem into a Momentum phase followed by an Energy phase is essential on AP Mechanics FRQs.

title: Translational-to-Rotational Dictionary
bulletsLatex: Every constant-acceleration linear equation maps 1-to-1 to rotation ($x \to \theta$, $v \to \omega$, $a \to \alpha$).

Use the right-hand rule: curl your fingers in the direction of rotation to find $\boldsymbol{\omega}$. If speeding up, $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ is parallel to $\boldsymbol{\omega}$; if slowing down, $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ is opposite $\boldsymbol{\omega}$.
trapLatex: Exam Trap: All points on a rigid rotating body share the SAME $\omega$ and $\alpha$, even though $v_t = r\omega$ and $a_t = r\alpha$ scale with radius $r$.

title: Torque, $\tau = I\alpha$, and Rotational Work
bulletsLatex: When a string unwinds without slipping from a pulley of radius $R$, the string's linear acceleration is coupled by $a = R\alpha$.
Rotational work is $W = \int \tau\,d\theta$ and instantaneous rotational power is $P = \tau\omega$.
trapLatex: Exam Trap: A massive pulley ($I > 0$) accelerating an attached block MUST have unequal tensions on its two sides ($T_2 \ne T_1$) to provide the net torque $\tau_{\text{net}} = (T_2 - T_1)R = I\alpha$.

promptLatex: A truck drives on the $xy$-plane in the $+y$-direction and applies its brakes, slowing down. In what direction does the angular acceleration vector $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ of its wheels point?
explanationLatex: By the right-hand rule, wheels rolling in the $+y$-direction have angular velocity $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ pointing in the $-x$-direction. Because the wheels are slowing down, $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ points opposite $\boldsymbol{\omega}$, which is $+x$.

promptLatex: A centrifuge rotor starts from rest, accelerates at constant $+\alpha$ for $\Delta t_1$, spins at constant angular speed for $\Delta t_2$, and slows down at $-\alpha$ until stopping. What is its total angular displacement $\Delta\theta$?
explanationLatex: By symmetry, deceleration also takes $\Delta t_1$. Total displacement is $\Delta\theta = \frac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta t_1^2 + (\alpha\Delta t_1)\Delta t_2 + \frac{1}{2}\alpha\Delta t_1^2 = \alpha\Delta t_1(\Delta t_1 + \Delta t_2)$.

promptLatex: A uniform rod of mass $m$, length $L$, and rotational inertia $I = \frac{1}{3}mL^2$ is pivoted without friction at one end and released from rest from a horizontal position. What is its initial angular acceleration $\alpha_0$?
explanationLatex: Gravity acts at the center of mass ($r = L/2$), producing initial torque $\tau_0 = mg(L/2) = I\alpha_0 = \left(\frac{1}{3}mL^2\right)\alpha_0 \implies \alpha_0 = \frac{3g}{2L}$.

promptLatex: A uniform rod of mass $m$, length $L$, and $I = \frac{1}{3}mL^2$ pivoted at one end swings down from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular speed $\omega$ as it passes through the vertical position?
explanationLatex: The center of mass drops by $h = L/2$. Conservation of energy gives $mg\left(\frac{L}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{3}mL^2\right)\omega^2 \implies \omega = \sqrt{\frac{3g}{L}}$.

promptLatex: When the pivoted uniform rod ($I = \frac{1}{3}mL^2$) released from horizontal swings through the **exact vertical position**, what is the tangential linear acceleration $a_t$ of its bottom tip?

promptLatex: A block of mass $m$ hangs from a string wrapped around a uniform solid disk pulley of mass $M$, radius $R$, and $I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$. When released from rest, what is the downward linear acceleration $a$ of the block?
explanationLatex: For the block: $mg - T = ma$. For the pulley: $TR = I\alpha = \frac{1}{2}MR^2(a/R) \implies T = \frac{1}{2}Ma$. Adding equations gives $mg = (m + \frac{1}{2}M)a$.

promptLatex: A motor applies an angle-dependent torque $\tau(\theta) = \tau_0 \cos\theta$ to a flywheel as it rotates from $\theta = 0$ to $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}$. How much work does the motor perform?
explanationLatex: $W = \int_0^{\pi/2} \tau_0\cos\theta\,d\theta = \tau_0\left[\sin\theta\right]_0^{\pi/2} = \tau_0(1 - 0) = \tau_0$.

explanationLatex: The frictional torque is $\tau = fR$, so instantaneous rotational power is $P = \tau\omega = fR\omega$.

promptLatex: A wheel starts from rest ($\omega(0) = 0$) with time-dependent angular acceleration $\alpha(t) = 6t - 2\text{ rad/s}^2$. Through what net angle $\Delta\theta$ does it rotate between $t = 0$ and $t = 2\text{ s}$?

promptLatex: A uniform solid cylinder of mass $M$, radius $R$, and $I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$ unwinds downward like a yo-yo from a vertical string attached to the ceiling. What is the tension $T$ in the string as it falls?

promptLatex: Order the steps to derive the acceleration $a$ of block $m_1$ on a frictionless horizontal table attached to hanging mass $m_2$ over a uniform disk pulley of mass $M$, radius $R$, and $I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$:

Apply the no-slip string constraint $\alpha = \frac{a}{R}$ to get $T_2 - T_1 = \frac{1}{2}Ma$
Add all three force equations to eliminate $T_1$ and $T_2$: $a = \frac{m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2 + \frac{1}{2}M}$
explanationLatex: Notice that a massive pulley simply adds its effective rotational mass ($I/R^2 = \frac{1}{2}M$) to the total inertia in the denominator.
